      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cholesterol</span></span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> to make hormones, vitamin D, and substances that help you digest foods. Your body makes all the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> it needs. <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cholesterol</span></span> is also found in foods from animal sources, such as egg yolks, meat, and cheese.</p><p>If you have too much <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> in your blood, it can combine with other substances in the blood to form plaque. Plaque sticks to the walls of your arteries. This buildup of plaque is known as atherosclerosis. It can lead to coronary artery disease, a condition in which your coronary arteries become narrow or even blocked.</p>What are HDL, LDL, and VLDL?<p>HDL, LDL, and VLDL are lipoproteins. They are a combination of fat (lipid) and protein. The lipids need to be attached to the proteins so they can move through the blood. Different types of lipoproteins have different purposes:</p><ul><li>HDL stands for <span class="qt0">high</span>-density lipoprotein. It is sometimes called "good" <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> because it helps your body get rid of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.  It carries <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> from other parts of your body back to your liver. Your liver then removes the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> from your body.</li><li>LDL stands for low-density lipoprotein. It is sometimes called "bad" <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> because a <span class="qt0">high</span> LDL <span class="qt3">level</span> leads to the buildup of plaque in your arteries.</li><li>VLDL stands for very low-density lipoprotein. Some people also call VLDL a "bad" <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> because it too contributes to the buildup of plaque in your arteries. But VLDL and LDL are different; VLDL mainly carries triglycerides and LDL mainly carries <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>?<p>The most common cause of <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> is an unhealthy lifestyle. This can include:</p><ul><li>Unhealthy eating habits, such as eating lots of saturated fats. These fats are found in red meats, full-fat dairy products, chocolate, some baked goods, and many deep-fried and processed foods.  Eating too much saturated fat can raise your LDL (bad) <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Lack of physical activity, with lots of sitting and little exercise. This lowers your HDL (good) <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Smoking, which lowers HDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, especially in women. It also raises your LDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Stress, which may raise <span class="qt3">levels</span> of certain hormones such as corticosteroids. These can cause your body to make more <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Drinking too much alcohol, which can raise your total <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">level</span>.</li></ul><p>Genetics may also cause people to have <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>. For example, familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is an inherited condition that causes very <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> in the blood. Other medical conditions and certain medicines may also raise LDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> or lower HDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span>.</p>What can raise my risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>?<p>A variety of things can raise your risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>:</p><ul><li>Age. Your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> tend to rise as you get older. Even though it is less common, younger people, including children and teens, can also have <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Sex. Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> total <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> than women. But after menopause, a woman's risk goes up. This happens because menopause lowers <span class="qt3">levels</span> of female hormones that may protect against <span class="qt0">high</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Family history. <span class="qt0">High</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> can run in families.</li><li>Other health conditions. Conditions such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease, HIV, and lupus can raise your risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.
</li><li>Medicines. Certain medicines can raise your <span class="qt3">level</span> of LDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> or lower your <span class="qt3">level</span> of HDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, including:
  <ul><li>Steroids</li><li>Some chemotherapy medicines</li><li>Medicines taken after an organ transplant</li><li>Medicines for certain heart conditions</li><li>Certain acne medicines</li></ul>
</li><li>Race or ethnicity. People from certain racial or ethnic groups may have an increased risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>. For example, Asian Americans are more likely to have <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> of LDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> than other groups. And non-Hispanic White people are more likely than other groups to have <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> of total <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Weight. Being overweight or having obesity raises your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">level</span>.</li></ul>What other health problems can <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> cause?<p>Undiagnosed or untreated <span class="qt0">high</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> can lead to serious health problems:</p><ul><li>If you have large deposits of plaque in your arteries, an area of plaque can rupture (break open). This can cause a blood clot to form on the surface of the plaque. If the clot becomes large enough, it can mostly or completely block blood flow in a coronary artery.</li><li>If the flow of oxygen-rich blood to your heart muscle is reduced or blocked, it can cause angina (chest pain) or a heart attack.</li><li>Plaque also can build up in other arteries in your body, including the arteries that bring oxygen-rich blood to your brain and limbs. This can lead to problems such as carotid artery disease, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> diagnosed?<p>There are usually no signs or symptoms that you have <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>. A blood test can measure your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span>. When and how often you should get this test depends on your age, risk factors, and family history.  The general recommendations are:</p><p>For people who are age 19 or younger:</p><ul><li>The first test should be between ages 9 to 11</li><li>Children should have the test again every 5 years</li><li>Some children may have this test starting at age 2 if there is a family history of <span class="qt0">high</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, heart attack, or stroke</li></ul><p>For people who are ages 20 to 65:</p><ul><li>Younger adults should have the test every 5 years</li><li>Men ages 45 to 65 and women ages 55 to 65 should have it every 1 to 2 years</li></ul><p>For people over age 65:</p><ul><li>They should be tested every year</li></ul>How can I lower my <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>?<p>You can lower your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> through heart-healthy lifestyle changes. They include a heart-healthy eating plan, weight management, and regular physical activity.</p><p>If the lifestyle changes alone do not lower your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> enough, you may also need to take medicines. There are several types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>-lowering medicines available, including statins. If you take medicines to lower your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, you still should continue with the lifestyle changes.</p><p>Some people with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) may receive a treatment called lipoprotein apheresis. This treatment uses a filtering machine to remove LDL <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> from the blood. Then the machine returns the rest of the blood back to the person.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Peripheral Arterial Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Arteriosclerosis of Extremities</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Claudication</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Intermittent Claudication</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PAD</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) happens when there is a narrowing of the blood vessels outside of your heart. The cause of PAD is atherosclerosis. This happens when plaque builds up on the walls of the arteries that supply blood to the arms and legs. Plaque is a substance made up of fat and <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>. It causes the arteries to narrow or become blocked. This can reduce or stop blood flow, usually to the legs. If severe enough, blocked blood flow can cause tissue death and can sometimes lead to amputation of the foot or leg.</p><p>The main risk factor for PAD is smoking. Other risk factors include older age and diseases like diabetes, <span class="qt0">high</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke.</p><p>Many people who have PAD don't have any symptoms. If you have symptoms, they may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, numbness, achiness, or heaviness in the leg muscles. This happens when walking or climbing stairs.</li><li>Weak or absent pulses in the legs or feet</li><li>Sores or wounds on the toes, feet, or legs that heal slowly, poorly, or not at all</li><li>A pale or bluish color to the skin</li><li>A lower temperature in one leg than the other leg</li><li>Poor nail growth on the toes and decreased hair growth on the legs</li><li>Erectile dysfunction, especially among men who have diabetes</li></ul><p>PAD can increase your risk of heart attack, stroke, and transient ischemic attack.</p><p>Doctors diagnose PAD with a physical exam and heart and imaging tests. Treatments include lifestyle changes, medicines, and sometimes surgery. Lifestyle changes include dietary changes, exercise, and efforts to lower <span class="qt0">high</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> and <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/howtopreventheartdisease.html">
      <content name="title">How to Prevent Heart Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Heart Disease Prevention</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Heart disease is the leading cause of the death in the United States. It is also a major cause of disability. But you can take steps to improve your health and help prevent heart disease. The first step is understanding your risk of heart disease. Your risk depends on many factors, some of which are changeable and others that are not. Learning about them and working on the things that you can change can lower your risk of heart disease.</p>What are the heart disease risk factors that I cannot change?<p>There are some risk factors for heart disease that you cannot change:</p><ul><li>Your age. Your risk of heart disease increases as you get older. The risk is <span class="qt0">higher</span> in:
  <ul><li>Men age 45 and older</li><li>Women age 55 and older</li></ul>
</li><li>Your sex. Some risk factors may affect heart disease risk differently in women than in men. For example: 
  <ul><li>The hormone estrogen provides women some protection against heart disease</li><li>Diabetes raises the risk of heart disease more in women than in men.</li></ul>
</li><li>Your race or ethnicity. Certain groups have <span class="qt0">higher</span> risks than others. For example:
  <ul><li>African Americans are more likely than Whites to die of heart disease, while Hispanic Americans are less likely to die of it</li><li>Asian Americans as a group have lower rates of heart disease than other groups, but South Asian Americans have <span class="qt0">higher</span> rates</li></ul>
</li><li>Your family history. You have a greater risk if you have a close family member who had heart disease at an early age, for example if:
  <ul><li>Your father or brother was diagnosed before age 55</li><li>Your mother or sister was diagnosed before age 65</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the heart disease risk factors I can change and what can I do to lower my risk?<p>There are many heart disease risk factors that you can change.  If you make these changes, you don't just help protect your heart. You can also improve your overall health and well-being.</p><p>You may have a lot of changes to make. If you need to, you can make the changes gradually, one at a time. What's most important is that you make them. Depending on your lifestyle, these changes could include:</p><ul><li>Controlling your blood pressure.<span class="qt0">High</span> blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart disease. It is important to get your blood pressure checked regularly - at least once a year for most adults, and more often if you have <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure. You can also take steps, including lifestyle changes, to prevent or control <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure.</li><li>Keeping your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> and triglyceride <span class="qt3">levels</span> under control:<ul><li><span class="qt0">High</span> <span class="qt3">levels</span> of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> can clog your arteries and raise your risk of coronary artery disease and heart attack. Lifestyle changes and medicines (if needed) can lower your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>.</li><li>Triglycerides are another type of fat in the blood. <span class="qt0">High</span>  <span class="qt3">levels</span> of triglyceride may also raise the risk of coronary artery disease, especially in women.</li></ul></li><li>Staying at a healthy weight. Being overweight or having obesity can increase your risk of heart disease. This is mostly because they are linked to other heart disease risk factors, including <span class="qt0">high</span> blood <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> and triglyceride <span class="qt3">levels</span>, <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure, and diabetes. Controlling your weight can lower these risks.</li><li>Eating a healthy diet. Try to limit saturated fats, foods <span class="qt0">high</span> in sodium (salt), and added sugars. Instead, eat plenty of fresh fruit, vegetables, and whole grains. The DASH diet is an example of an eating plan that can help you to lower your blood pressure and <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>, two things that can lower your risk of heart disease.</li><li>Getting regular physical activity. Regular physical activity has many benefits, including strengthening your heart and improving your circulation. It can also help you maintain a healthy weight and lower <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> and blood pressure. All of these can lower your risk of heart disease.</li><li>Limiting alcohol. Drinking too much alcohol can raise your blood pressure. It also adds extra calories, which may cause weight gain. Both of those raise your risk of heart disease. It's best not to drink, but if you do:
  <ul><li>Have no more than 2 drinks per day if you are a man.</li><li>Have no more than 1 drink per day if you are a woman.</li></ul>
</li><li>Not smoking. Cigarette smoking raises your blood pressure and puts you at <span class="qt0">higher</span> risk of heart attack and stroke. 
  <ul><li>If you do not smoke, don't start.</li><li> If you do smoke, quitting will lower your risk of heart disease. You can talk with your health care provider for help in finding the best way for you to quit.</li></ul>
</li><li>Managing stress.Stress is linked to heart disease in many ways. It can raise your blood pressure. Extreme stress can be a "trigger" for a heart attack. Also, some common ways of coping with stress, such as overeating, heavy drinking, and smoking, are bad for your heart. Some ways to help manage your stress include exercise, listening to music, focusing on something calm or peaceful, and meditating.</li><li>Managing diabetes. Having diabetes doubles your risk of diabetic heart disease. That is because over time, <span class="qt0">high</span> blood glucose (blood sugar) from diabetes can damage your blood vessels and the nerves that control your heart and blood vessels. So, it is important to get tested for diabetes, and if you have it, to keep it under control.</li><li>Getting enough sleep. If you don't get enough sleep, you raise your risk of <span class="qt0">high</span> blood pressure, obesity, and diabetes. Those three things can raise your risk of heart disease. To improve your sleep:
  <ul><li>If you are an adult, try to get 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night.</li><li>Make sure that you have good sleep habits, such as keeping a regular sleep schedule and creating a good sleeping environment in your bedroom.</li><li> If you have frequent sleep problems, contact your health care provider. One problem, sleep apnea, causes people to briefly stop breathing many times during sleep. This interferes with your ability to get a good rest and can raise your risk of heart disease. If you think you might have sleep apnea, ask your provider about having a sleep study. And if you do have sleep apnea, make sure that you get treatment for it.</li></ul>
</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/heartdiseases.html">

      <content name="FullSummary">What is heart disease?<p>Heart disease is a general term that includes many types of heart problems. It's a type of cardiovascular disease, which means heart and blood vessel disease.</p><p>Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, but there are ways to prevent and manage many types of heart disease.</p>What are the types of heart disease?<p>There are many different types of heart disease. Some you may be born with, called congenital heart disease. Other types develop during your lifetime.</p><p>Coronary artery disease (also called coronary heart disease) is the most common type of heart disease. It happens slowly over time when a sticky substance called plaque builds up in the arteries that supply your heart muscle with blood. The plaque narrows or blocks blood flow to the heart muscle and can lead to other heart problems:</p><ul><li>Angina - chest pain from lack of blood flow</li><li>Heart attacks - when part of the heart muscle dies from loss of blood flow</li><li>Heart failure - when your heart can't pump enough blood to meet your body's needs</li><li>Arrhythmia - a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat</li></ul><p>Other types of heart diseases may affect your heart valves or heart muscle (cardiomyopathy).</p>What causes heart diseases?<p>The causes of heart disease depend on the type of disease. Some possible causes include lifestyle, genetics, infections, medicines, and other diseases.</p>Who is more likely to develop heart diseases?<p>There are many different factors that can make you more likely to develop heart disease. Some of these factors you can change, but others you cannot.</p><ul><li>Age. Your risk of heart disease goes up as you get older.</li><li>Sex. Some factors may affect heart disease risk differently in women than in men.</li><li>Family history and genetics. A family history of early heart disease raises your risk. And research has shown that some genes are linked to a <span class="qt0">higher</span> risk of certain heart diseases.</li><li>Race/ethnicity. Heart disease is the leading cause of death in most racial and ethnic groups in the United States. However, certain groups have <span class="qt0">higher</span> risks than others. This includes Black people, White people, and American Indian/Alaska Native people.</li><li>Lifestyle habits. Over time, unhealthy lifestyle habits can raise your risk of heart disease. These can include: 
	<ul><li>Eating a diet <span class="qt0">high</span> in saturated fats, refined carbohydrates, and salt.</li><li>Not getting enough physical activity.</li><li>Drinking too much alcohol.</li><li>Smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke.</li><li>Too much stress.</li></ul>
</li><li>Having other medical conditions can raise your risk of heart diseases. These conditions include:
	<ul><li><span class="qt0">High</span> blood pressure.</li><li><span class="qt0">High</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span>.</li><li>Diabetes.</li><li>Obesity.</li><li>Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.</li><li>Chronic kidney disease.</li><li>Metabolic syndrome.</li></ul>
</li></ul>What are the symptoms of heart disease?<p>Your symptoms will depend on the type of heart disease you have. You may not have symptoms at first. In some cases, you may not know you have heart disease until you have a complication such as a heart attack.</p>How are heart diseases diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have heart disease, your health care provider will:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had heart disease</li><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Likely run heart tests and blood tests</li></ul><p>In some cases, your provider may refer you to a cardiologist (a doctor who specializes in heart diseases) for tests, diagnosis, and care.</p>What are the treatments for heart disease?<p>Treatment plans for heart disease depend on the type of heart disease you have, how serious your symptoms are, and what other health conditions you have. Possible treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Heart-healthy lifestyle changes</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Procedures or surgeries</li><li>Cardiac rehabilitation</li></ul>Can heart diseases be prevented?<p>You may be able to lower your risk of certain heart diseases by making heart-healthy lifestyle changes  and managing any other medical conditions you have.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">Levels</span>: What You Need to Know</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Combined Hyperlipidemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Dysbetalipoproteinemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Familial Hypercholesterolemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypercholesterolemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hyperlipidemia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cholesterol</span></span> is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases.</p>How do you measure <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span>?<p>A blood test called a lipoprotein or lipid panel can measure your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> <span class="qt3">levels</span>. Before the test, you'll usually need to fast (not eat or drink anything but water) for 9 to 12 hours. Follow the instructions your health care provider gives you.</p><p>The test gives information about your:</p><ul><li>Total <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span>. This is a measure of the total amount of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cholesterol</span></span> in your blood.
